opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, James. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won't be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Very glad to. I should warn you, I've never used one of these AI programs, so I'm speaking from what I read and what my students hand in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, as I do in faculty meetings, that a machine which produces fluent text is not the same as a mind that understands the past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even in this mild version, I see essays that are smooth and empty. Students skip the slow work of reading sources, and that slow work is the whole point of history.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go back to handwritten exams and long conversations in my office. Make students show me their notes from the archive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Irritated, more than afraid.

S0.say: A machine that produces fluent text is not a mind that understands the past.
S0.think: Even now he sees smooth, empty essays from students skipping the slow work of reading sources.
S0.do: Brings back handwritten exams and office conversations, and asks to see archive notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say universities should defend careful thought, slowly and stubbornly, the way we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing. I'm tenured and a year or two from retiring. Fewer young scholars hired, though, would mean fewer people to carry the subject on. That saddens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Write to the dean about protecting junior posts in the humanities. Finish my last book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, but I'm not frightened.

S1.say: Universities should defend careful thought, slowly and stubbornly, as always.
S1.think: He's tenured and near retirement, but fewer young scholars means fewer people to carry the subject on.
S1.do: Writes to the dean about protecting junior humanities posts and finishes his last book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments should regulate this firmly and protect the people losing work. I've believed in a strong state my whole life, and this is why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office work being automated will make parents ask why their children should study history at all. My department would shrink. I'd retire before it reached me, but my younger colleagues wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used these tools yourself. How sure are you about what they can do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very sure, if I'm honest. I may be underestimating them, or overestimating them. I'm judging by the essays, and that's a narrow window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speak at the faculty senate. Sign the letters. Help two of my younger colleagues apply elsewhere, where the subject is safer, if such a place exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A heaviness. For the field, not myself.

S2.say: Governments should regulate this firmly and protect people losing work.
S2.think: Parents will ask why their children should study history, and his department would shrink. He'd retire first, but younger colleagues wouldn't.
S2.do: Speaks at the faculty senate, signs open letters and helps younger colleagues apply elsewhere.
S2.feel: A heaviness for the field, not himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say plainly that a society which hands its thinking to machines owned by a few companies is in danger. The gains belong to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If machines match skilled professionals at thinking work, many will ask what a university is for. The humanities would be cut first. And people would stop doing the slow, hard thinking themselves. That's the loss I fear most, more than jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retire on schedule, but keep teaching evening classes in town for anyone who wants to read and argue about history. Give more to the parties pushing for public ownership of the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grieved. Worried for how people will think.

S3.say: A society that hands its thinking to machines owned by a few companies is in danger. The gains belong to everyone.
S3.think: Universities would be questioned and the humanities cut first, but his deeper fear is people giving up slow, hard thinking.
S3.do: Retires on schedule, teaches evening history classes in town and gives more to parties pushing for public ownership of the gains.
S3.feel: Grieved, worried about how people will think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we are seeing the largest shift in working life since the factories came, and history tells us those shifts end in either reform or upheaval. We should choose reform.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me the robots are beside the point. My wife and I have our savings and my pension. But I've read enough history to know what happens when ordinary people lose their place. It isn't gentle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same as before. Write something for the local paper on what past upheavals teach us, because that's the one useful thing I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about myself. Uneasy about the country.

S4.say: Shifts this large end in reform or upheaval. We should choose reform.
S4.think: The robots don't touch him, but history tells him what happens when ordinary people lose their place.
S4.do: Keeps his plans and writes for the local paper on what past upheavals teach.
S4.feel: Calm about himself, uneasy about the country.
